items.title: ANEG Foundation launches climate awareness and tree-planting project at Amedeka
items.description: The ANEG Foundation has launched a climate awareness and tree-planting initiative at Amedeka, bringing together 35 participants to promote environmental sustainability and encourage young people to take an active role in climate action. The exercise, held on Friday, October 23, 2026, involved climate advocates, Environmental Club students and members of the foundation who planted fruit trees on a designated piece of land. The seedlings included pawpaw, mango, lime and soursop, selected to expand green spaces and promote the environmental benefits of tree planting in local communities. The initiative forms part of the foundation’s efforts to advance climate action, protect the environment and encourage youth participation in building greener and healthier communities. The exercise began at 9:30 a.m. and ended at 11:00 a.m., with participants working together to plant the seedlings and raise awareness about the importance of trees in addressing climate change. Monitoring to support tree survival Beyond the planting exercise, the ANEG Foundation says it will conduct periodic visits to the site to monitor the growth and survival of the seedlings and ensure they receive the necessary care. The foundation says the monitoring process is intended to improve the seedlings’ chances of survival and ensure the project delivers lasting environmental benefits. It plans to extend the initiative to Natriku, Lubuse and Kasunya as part of efforts to reach more communities with its environmental activities. Partners support climate initiative The foundation has expressed appreciation to residents of Amedeka, climate advocates, Environmental Club students and other participants for their contributions to the exercise. It also acknowledged Fairtrade and Golden Exotics Limited for sponsoring the initiative. The ANEG Foundation says the project reflects its broader commitment to community-led environmental protection and inspiring young people to become advocates for climate action. It hopes the initiative will encourage a culture of tree planting and responsible environmental stewardship, with continued monitoring and care expected to be central to its long-term success.

items.title: Langues nationales au Parlement : comprendre la démarche pédagogique du président Dansa Kourouma (Par Nafadji Sory Condé)
items.description: La déclaration du président de l'Assemblée nationale, Dr Dansa Kourouma, selon laquelle l'exercice du droit des députés à s'exprimer dans les langues nationales doit être « strictement encadré », mérite une analyse juridique et sociolinguistique dépassionnée. Certains pourraient y voir une restriction à la reconnaissance constitutionnelle des langues nationales. Pourtant, il convient de distinguer la consécration d'un droit constitutionnel et les modalités pratiques de son exercice au sein d'une institution parlementaire. La Constitution reconnaît le droit, mais prévoit son encadrement L'article 5 de la Constitution du 26 septembre 2025 consacre les langues nationales et le français comme langues officielles de la République de Guinée, tout en maintenant le français comme langue de travail. Il prévoit également que l'État assure la promotion de l'enseignement des langues nationales et garantit la traduction des lois et actes officiels dans ces langues. Surtout, cet article renvoie expressément à une loi organique pour définir ses modalités d'application. Cette précision est fondamentale : le statut officiel des langues nationales est constitutionnellement acquis, mais sa pleine mise en œuvre institutionnelle nécessite un encadrement juridique, organisationnel et technique. Les règlements intérieurs des deux chambres prévoient déjà l'utilisation des langues nationales L'article 79 du Règlement intérieur de l'Assemblée nationale et l'article 81 de celui du Sénat organisent l'utilisation des langues nationales dans les débats parlementaires. Ces dispositions maintiennent le français comme langue d'usage des séances, tout en prévoyant, sous certaines conditions, la possibilité pour les parlementaires de s'exprimer dans une langue nationale. Elles instituent également le principe d'un système de traduction simultanée destiné à garantir la compréhension des débats et l'égalité de participation. Ces dispositions démontrent que l'encadrement de l'utilisation des langues nationales n'est pas une initiative personnelle du président de l'Assemblée nationale, mais une exigence inscrite dans les textes régissant le fonctionnement parlementaire. Comprendre la démarche du président Dr Dansa Kourouma Le président de l'Assemblée nationale a la responsabilité de faire fonctionner efficacement l'institution, dans le respect de la Constitution et du Règlement intérieur. Or, comment garantir la qualité des débats si plusieurs députés interviennent dans différentes langues nationales sans dispositif de traduction opérationnel ? Comment assurer la compréhension des interventions, la fidélité des comptes rendus et l'égalité des parlementaires devant l'information ? Ces interrogations expliquent la nécessité d'un encadrement rigoureux. Le droit d'un député à s'exprimer dans une langue nationale doit être concilié avec celui de ses collègues à comprendre son intervention. C'est dans cette logique que je comprends la pédagogie institutionnelle du président Dr Dansa Kourouma : il ne s'agit pas de remettre en cause un acquis constitutionnel, mais d'organiser son exercice dans des conditions garantissant l'efficacité du travail parlementaire. Le Code linguistique et la traduction simultanée : deux étapes décisives La future loi organique portant Code linguistique de la République de Guinée devra préciser les modalités générales d'application de l'article 5 de la Constitution. Son adoption permettra notamment de clarifier l'utilisation des langues officielles dans les institutions publiques, les obligations de traduction et les garanties des droits linguistiques. Toutefois, son absence ne suspend ni la Constitution ni les dispositions déjà applicables des règlements intérieurs des deux chambres. Parallèlement, l'installation d'un système de traduction simultanée, accompagnée de la formation d'interprètes parlementaires qualifiés, constituera une avancée déterminante. Dès que ce dispositif sera opérationnel, les possibilités d'intervention dans les langues nationales pourront être considérablement élargies. Il faudra néanmoins éviter que les contraintes techniques ou l'attente du Code linguistique ne deviennent des motifs de report indéfini de l'exercice des droits déjà reconnus. Une démarche progressive plutôt qu'une opposition aux langues nationales En définitive, la position du président Dr Dansa Kourouma peut être comprise comme une démarche de responsabilité institutionnelle visant à concilier trois impératifs : Le respect de la Constitution et des droits linguistiques des parlementaires ; L'application des règlements intérieurs de l'Assemblée nationale et du Sénat ; La continuité, l'efficacité et la qualité des travaux parlementaires. Cette démarche mérite d'être comprise et accompagnée, à condition qu'elle s'inscrive dans un calendrier concret de mise en œuvre du multilinguisme parlementaire. Conclusion La Guinée a franchi une étape historique en consacrant constitutionnellement ses langues nationales comme langues officielles. Il reste désormais à transformer cette reconnaissance juridique en pratiques institutionnelles effectives. La Constitution a consacré le principe, les règlements intérieurs ont organisé les premières modalités, le futur Code linguistique devra compléter le dispositif et la traduction simultanée permettra d'en assurer l'effectivité. C'est pourquoi je considère que la démarche du président Dr Dansa Kourouma, loin d'être nécessairement une remise en cause de la co-officialité des langues nationales, peut être interprétée comme une volonté d'en garantir une application progressive, ordonnée et efficace. L'essentiel est d'encadrer sans exclure, d'organiser sans retarder indéfiniment et de promouvoir nos langues nationales sans compromettre l'efficacité de nos institutions. Nafadji Sory CONDÉ Sociolinguiste, spécialiste des langues africaines et des politiques linguistiques et éducatives. items.title: Chris Hesse’s film legacy takes centre stage at UniMAC-IFT
items.description: UniMAC-IFT will screen historic footage of Ghana’s independence and early nationhood on 30th October, highlighting veteran cinematographer Rev. Dr Chris Hesse’s efforts to preserve the country’s audiovisual heritage. Ghana’s history has survived in books, monuments and the memories of those who lived through its defining moments. Yet another record of the nation’s past, one capable of bringing its political struggles, cultural expressions and national ambitions vividly back to life, remains vulnerable: the films that captured Ghana as it emerged from colonial rule. For veteran cinematographer Rev. Dr Chris Hesse, preserving these moving images has become a defining part of his legacy. His work safeguarding footage associated with Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah, has helped keep alive a visual record of the country’s formative years, at a time when the survival of historical film collections has become an urgent cultural concern. That legacy will come into focus on Friday, 30 October, when the University of Media, Arts and Communication’s Institute of Film and Television (UniMAC-IFT), in partnership with the UNESCO Ghana Office, screens historic films to mark the World Day for Audiovisual Heritage. The event, to be held at the institute’s television studio, will feature footage documenting Ghana’s independence celebrations, the inauguration of the First Republican Parliament, the opening of Tema Harbour and Nkrumah’s international engagements. Head of the UNESCO Office in Ghana, H.E. Edmond Moukala, is expected to deliver the keynote address, while Hesse will attend as special guest of honour. The screening offers more than an opportunity to revisit historical events. It raises a fundamental question about who preserves a nation’s visual memory, how that memory is protected and whether future generations will have meaningful access to it. Among the films scheduled for screening are Freedom for Ghana , The Inauguration of the First Republican Parliament , Ghana National Anthem , Progress at Akosombo , Industrial Development in Ghana and Roots of Highlife . The programme also includes Africa Reborn: Birth of the OAU and footage of Nkrumah’s overseas visits. Collectively, the films document a country defining its political identity, developing its infrastructure and establishing relationships across a newly independent Africa and the wider world. They also offer researchers, educators, filmmakers and younger audiences access to original images that can deepen their understanding of events often encountered only through written accounts. The significance of such records becomes clearer when their vulnerability is considered. Many historic productions were recorded on celluloid film, a medium susceptible to deterioration when exposed to unsuitable storage conditions. Preserving these materials requires specialised handling, appropriate environmental conditions, technical expertise and, increasingly, digitisation to facilitate access and support long-term preservation. Hesse’s archive illustrates both the value of preservation and the consequences of leaving it to chance. His collection contains more than 1,000 reels of footage documenting Ghana’s independence era and the wider African liberation movement. The story of these recordings has gained renewed attention through The Eyes of Ghana , a documentary directed by filmmaker Ben Proudfoot that follows Hesse’s efforts to preserve and bring this historical material to wider audiences. The concern extends beyond whether the reels physically survive. Historical footage must also be properly identified, catalogued, documented and made accessible under appropriate copyright and licensing arrangements. Without these systems, valuable recordings can remain effectively invisible, even when they have escaped physical destruction. For Ghana, that represents a cultural and educational loss. Footage of political ceremonies can help historians examine the country’s early institutions, while recordings of infrastructure projects can illuminate changing development priorities. Music and cultural performances preserve aspects of social life that written documents may not fully convey. The importance of protecting these records also connects with Ghana’s broader efforts to safeguard its cultural heritage. In December 2025, UNESCO inscribed highlife music and dance on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognising a tradition whose rhythms, lyrics and performances reflect Ghanaian life and identity. Preserving audiovisual records can complement such efforts by retaining the images and sounds through which cultural practices, artistic traditions and historical experiences have been expressed and transmitted. The potential benefits also reach the creative economy. Properly preserved and accessible archives can support documentary production, historical films, educational programming and exhibitions. With clear access and licensing frameworks, they can also create opportunities for collaboration between archivists, researchers and contemporary filmmakers seeking to tell Ghanaian stories through authentic historical material. The World Day for Audiovisual Heritage, observed annually on 27 October, draws attention to the need to safeguard films, sound recordings, radio broadcasts and other audiovisual documents. This year’s screening, themed “Your Window to the World”, will bring that international message into a Ghanaian context, connecting the preservation of historical records with the responsibility to make them available to the public. For UniMAC-IFT, the event is an opportunity to place audiovisual preservation at the centre of conversations about film education and the future of Ghana’s screen industries. It also provides a platform to consider how institutions can work with professionals and other stakeholders to protect collections that hold national significance. Ultimately, Hesse’s legacy poses a challenge that extends beyond one cinematographer or one collection of films. His work demonstrates the value of preserving history, but it also raises questions about the institutional support, resources and long-term planning needed to ensure that the responsibility does not rest on individual commitment alone. When the historic footage returns to the screen in Accra, audiences will see more than images of a country’s past. They will encounter evidence of the ambitions, struggles and cultural expressions that helped shape modern Ghana. Whether those images remain available for future generations will depend on what the country does to preserve them today.

items.title: Vice President calls for stronger role for queen mothers in advancing women’s rights
items.description: Vice President Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang has urged queen mothers to use their influence to strengthen women’s participation in community decision-making. She said traditional leaders play an important role in advancing gender equality and creating opportunities for women to contribute to community development. The Vice President made the call at the Yokama Ligbi (Ideal Woman Day) celebration, held as part of the 133rd Ngmayem Festival of the Manya Krobo Traditional Area in the Eastern Region. She stressed the need to move beyond policy commitments and ensure that measures designed to empower women translate into tangible improvements in their lives. Professor Opoku-Agyemang cited the Social Protection Act 2025, the Social Protection Regulations and the Affirmative Action Regulations 2026, launched earlier this month, as examples of efforts to strengthen support for vulnerable groups and promote equal opportunities. She urged queen mothers to help ensure that women were not excluded from decisions affecting their families and communities. The Vice President also highlighted the proposed Women Development Bank, which is expected to improve access to finance for women who face difficulties securing loans from traditional financial institutions. She said women traders and farmers often struggled to obtain credit because they lacked the collateral or financial records required by lenders. Improving access to finance, she said, would help women expand their businesses and contribute more effectively to Ghana’s economic development. On education, Professor Opoku-Agyemang said the Free Senior High School programme was helping to remove barriers that prevented girls from accessing secondary education. She, however, emphasised that families, schools, traditional authorities and communities must work together to guide young people and prepare them for the future. The Vice President also encouraged young people to remain curious, question existing assumptions and be willing to learn and reconsider their views. Professor Opoku-Agyemang was honoured during the celebration and expressed appreciation to the chiefs, queen mothers, elders and people of the Manya Krobo Traditional Area for the recognition. Yokama Ligbi, meaning Ideal Woman Day, is an annual feature of the Ngmayem Festival that celebrates Krobo women who have distinguished themselves through professional achievements, character and contributions to culture and community development. The initiative was introduced in 2003 by the Paramount Chief of the Manya Krobo Traditional Area, Nene Sakite II, five years after his enstoolment as Konor. Traditionally held on the third day of the week-long festival, the celebration features traditional attire and performances of the Klama dance, highlighting the cultural heritage of the Krobo people.

items.title: Chromebook scheme
items.description: THE government’s plan to distribute 500,000 Chromebooks to students over two years could help narrow Pakistan’s digital divide. The devices, which will come with MiFi internet connectivity, are meant for students handpicked under the scheme. In a country where access to computers and reliable internet still depends heavily on family income and location, that matters. A student who cannot afford a laptop should not be locked out of online learning, digital skills or job opportunities. But the value of the scheme will depend on how it is carried out. The state should publish clear eligibility criteria, ensure that poorer students are not crowded out by those who already have devices, and explain how the refurbished Chromebooks will be procured, tested and distributed. The total cost should also be disclosed, along with safeguards against political influence in selecting recipients and suppliers. There should also be a plan for repairs, replacement and technical support. A device that stops working after a few months, or cannot connect reliably outside major cities, will do little to close the gap it was meant to address. More importantly, access to hardware is only one part of Pakistan’s education problem . A Chromebook cannot compensate for weak teaching, poor literacy, overcrowded classrooms or schools without dependable electricity and internet access. Nor will handing out devices automatically improve learning. Teachers need training to use digital tools well, students need access to useful content, and schools need systems that can blend technology with ordinary classroom instruction. The government should therefore set measurable goals for the scheme: whether students use the devices regularly for learning, whether their digital skills improve, and whether this leads to better educational outcomes. Independent evaluation would help determine if the programme deserves expansion. There is also a case for giving students in remote and low-income areas greater weight, since they stand to benefit most from access they currently lack. Pakistan has launched laptop schemes before; what matters now is whether this one produces more than a distribution ceremony. Technology can widen opportunity, but only when it is tied to good teaching, reliable connectivity and clear educational purpose. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

items.title: Séné Diallo, l’artiste affable aux frasques calculées, s’en est allé ! (Par Hassane Hilal Sylla)
items.description: Screenshot " data-large-file="https://i0.wp.com/mediaguinee.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_0762.jpeg?fit=1024%2C758&ssl=1" /> Une voix s’est tue. Une joie s’est éteinte. L’artiste a joué son dernier acte. ———————————————— Je fis la connaissance de Séné Diallo, l’enfant de Fria et de Sombori, grâce à Radio Nostalgie Guinée dans les années 2006. Il nous enseignait alors à travers ses émissions l’art du punch d’un animateur à l’image d’ABD, le choix des mots pour toucher l’auditeur et la créativité d’un homme de média inimitable. Sa voix et sa verve naturelle m’ont inspiré lorsque, deux ans plus tard, à la fin de mes études universitaires, je décidais de me lancer dans le journalisme et la présentation télévisée. Si je n’ai pas réussi là où Séné Diallo excellait en véritable maître, j’ai néanmoins retenu de lui le modèle expressif et la brillante aisance de l’animateur qu’il était. Séné Diallo demeurait ainsi, à mes yeux, une icône immuable. ———————————————– Ma rencontre avec celui qui était devenu mon icône, Séné Diallo, que j’appelais désormais affectueusement « le Fory », fut à la fois remarquable et pleine de considération. C’était à Djoma Média. Moi qui le regardais comme on contemple une étoile, avec admiration, je découvrais un homme qui, en retour, m’accueillait avec beaucoup de considération. Il nous témoignait une considération si naturelle, si déconcertante parfois, qu’on aurait presque pu croire qu’il se jouait de nous, tant son ouverture et sa simplicité étaient désarmantes. Séné Diallo était un homme affable. ———————————————– L’artiste s’en est allé. Il laisse derrière lui ses enfants, qu’il préparait à affronter cette vie d’aujourd’hui, où la joie semblait être son maître mot. Si je suis profondément peiné par sa disparition brutale, je n’ose imaginer la douleur de ses héritiers, désormais contraints d’apprendre à avancer dans la vie sans père, nirepère. ———————————————– Ce lundi noir, Ce mois d’octobre sombre, Cet homme dont la vie se conjugue désormais au passé devrait encore nous enseigner, par le souvenir qu’il nous laisse, la profondeur de l’amour qu’il portait à chacun de nous. À travers son imagination débordante, ses frasques calculées et son sens élevé de l’amitié, il nous a appris à aimer, à rire et à vivre en paix. ———————————————– Séné Diallo, l’artiste, va en paix ! Qu’Allah, dans Son infinie miséricorde, l’accueille auprès de Lui. Que Sa volonté soit faite. L’article Séné Diallo, l’artiste affable aux frasques calculées, s’en est allé ! (Par Hassane Hilal Sylla) est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Democrats Are Sounding More Like Republicans
items.description: For a long time now, Democrats have mostly avoided the language of moral judgment. The average American wasn’t alive when Jimmy Carter inveighed against the “self-indulgence and consumption” of his fellow citizens, and even that seemed to be an aberration. Until this election cycle, that is. Now Senator Chris Murphy is worried about “America’s spiritual unraveling,” and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senate candidate in Michigan, regularly calls out the “moral rot” of the Trump administration. Raphael Warnock and Cory Booker speak in sermon-ese, and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro likes to slap a lectern and say , “I know my Bible!” My favorite example, though, is the Texas Senate candidate James Talarico’s campaign slogan, lifted straight from the gospels with a wink at Jesus’s rebuke to the money changers: “It’s time to start flipping tables.” This is not about finding religion—though faith is a factor : Talarico is one of 12 Democrats who have run for federal office this year who are pastors, former clergy, or seminary students. What is more widespread, rather, is a sudden willingness to speak in universal and absolute terms about norms of behavior—about right and wrong. Post-Carter Democrats have usually presented themselves as the party of technocratic solutions, fetishizing policy or the pragmatic value of—Bill Clinton’s favorite word— triangulation . Now their message sounds like it’s being delivered from a pulpit rather than a bureaucrat’s desk, a moral imperative best summed up in the title of Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear’s new memoir: Go and Do Likewise . I hold one man responsible for this altered tone, and it’s not Jesus. When you have a president whose worldview resembles something out of Squid Game ; who has talked about being constrained only by his “ own morality,” whatever that may be; who characterized soldiers who died for a cause larger than themselves as “suckers” and “losers,” then political physics suggests that the pendulum will soon swing in the other direction. There is a crude and simple way for Democrats to respond to Donald Trump’s flamboyant amorality, and we’re seeing some of it in action. They might simply label everything that he has done (immigration crackdowns, elective wars, tariffs) as “evil,” strongly implying that they are the corrective, the “good.” The Christian right often deploys the language of morality in this Manichaean fashion—it’s the logic by which the evangelist Jerry Falwell once declared Trump to be a “good, moral person.” But the concept quickly cancels itself out when it becomes just another rhetorical weapon. At a rally in Michigan this summer, J. D. Vance said there was something “very, very evil” about El-Sayed —who responded by saying, “Let me tell you what’s evil,” and then cataloged the administration’s policies. To truly name and confront evil—not as just a synonym for things we don’t like but as a foundational concept deeper than day-to-day politics—is, to put it mildly, hard. For people not inclined toward religion, the idea of an ultimate badness seems impossible to extract from theology (an objection I’ll get to). And for those who do have faith, the word might feel too heavy, too spiritually fraught, and too absolute to toss around on the profane battleground of politics. And yet, a working definition of evil might be what we need to recognize what has gone so askew, not just in the current administration but in society, in us. Susan Neiman , the moral philosopher, has titled her new book Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era , but she is quick to explain, on the second page, that “this is not a book about Donald Trump.” What she means is that someone who proudly says that he could shoot someone on 5th Avenue without any repercussions couldn’t triumph in our political system unless the ground was already prepared for him. The evil she wants us to get comfortable naming is more pervasive than just one man or party. And Democrats rushing to counter Trump with righteousness should pay attention. [ Read: Is anything morally obvious anymore? ] Neiman, who has lived mostly in Berlin since the 1980s and served as the director of the Einstein Forum, is a prominent defender of the battered ideals of the Enlightenment. In her books, she has maintained that reason, moral judgment, and the aspiration to universal human dignity—legacies of the early modern thinkers—are worth preserving. They just need some blood flowing through them again. Evil, in particular, has been her special interest for a long time; it was the subject of her most influential book, Evil in Modern Thought , published in 2002. Like Hannah Arendt in her famous book Eichmann in Jerusalem , Neiman is less interested in evil as the province of monsters than as a possibility embedded in ordinary human life. Arendt diagnosed the Nazi bureaucrat Adolf Eichmann with “thoughtlessness,” a habit that can turn mass murder into an administrative task. Neiman builds on this idea in her new book, which is a short, slightly rushed summary of her thinking meant to meet the urgency of the moment. Thoughtlessness is possible, she argues, when morality itself is seen as a joke, as cringe , and when acting out of moral conviction is perceived as a game for suckers and losers. What she names as “the evil that threatens us most today” is “the idea that nothing is evil.” This might sound like a hollow tautology, but to put it another way, she is worried about moral vacuousness. What has shoved aside the notion of good and evil is an ideology of self-interest, which posits that humans are merely animals preoccupied with satisfying their individual needs and increasing their power over others. Or, to borrow the words of that great philosopher Stephen Miller , the idea that “iron laws of the world since the beginning of time” dictate that the planet is governed by “strength,” “force,” and “power” alone. Neiman would identify the kind of thinking Miller expressed as evil: “The signal evil of our age is the belief that self-interest is all that moves us, and ideas of justice are self-deluded hype. Evil actions are those that deny the possibility of morality.” This ideology of self-interest has become so firmly implanted in modern society that someone like Trump could come across simply as the guy who says the quiet part out loud. In her explanation for how we got here, Neiman distributes blame along the entire political spectrum. Her brief against the left is one of negligence. Gradually, beginning in the 1960s, the left abandoned the language of universal principles for a politics focused on identity and power (one of Neiman’s recent books was called Left Is Not Woke ). In place of an objective idea of justice, liberal and leftist thought has resembled something akin to the French philosopher Michel Foucault’s vision of a world of struggle, in which various groups and institutions vie to define reality in terms preferential to themselves. This relativism made morality seem not just irrelevant but also a kind of childish fantasy. And as the left turned away from Enlightenment universalism, the right propagated an equally cold and cutthroat idea, which has shaped how we think about human nature itself. The laissez-faire market fundamentalism promoted by Milton Friedman saw an unregulated market as leading to the best of all possible worlds. For all of the benefits of capitalism, this ethos of competitiveness, taken to its extreme, necessitated a picture of humans as essentially greedy. This idea that people are ruthlessly self-interested and rational, Homo economicus , was supposed to be the basis of a theoretical model, a speculation among early capitalist thinkers such as Adam Smith about how we might act if we were thinking only about maximizing our profit with minimal effort. Yet, Neiman argues, it became accepted not as theory but as truth—that we were “cold-hearted calculators,” as the economist Joseph E. Stiglitz put it. [ Read: What Stephen Miller gets wrong about human nature ] The result, Neiman writes, is a world in which it seems silly or irrelevant to suggest how things ought to be for all of us. Instead, we stomach all kinds of cruelty and corruption, lying and cynicism and shamelessness, because that’s just how people behave. This is ultimately what makes an absence of morality so dangerous, so soul crushing, so evil: It forecloses the possibility of goodness. Neiman’s diagnosis feels compelling to me, with one huge caveat. Reading her book, I had a nagging worry that there was no real way to fill this moral vacuum without some kind of faith. How do we regain a common reference point without a supreme being or a shared tradition to adjudicate behavior? Neiman understands that this is a problem, and her answer skirts around it. Whether you find her solution convincing will probably determine if the rest of her argument stands up for you. This is also where I think Democratic politicians eager to speak about morality might have something to learn. Her answer is, basically, trust your gut. Evil is something we all know when we see it, and we don’t need a thunderclap to signal its presence. “Evil is an idea that arises whenever the gap between the way the world is and the way the world ought to be becomes too big to bear alone,” Neiman writes. It’s the word you use to describe that moment “when your jaw begins to drop,” when you sense that “a line has been crossed.” Here are a few test cases from the past couple of years: What do you feel when considering the separation of children from their parents? What about the bombing of an Iranian school that killed 120 students? Or what about the estimated hundreds of thousands of deaths that resulted from cuts to USAID? I’ll tell you the feeling these events provoke in me. I call it moral nausea. Neiman would say that by recognizing this feeling of wrongness, of evil, we can claw our way back to an overarching sense of justice. This is the visceral level at which Democratic politicians—or any politician, really—could be talking about morality. Not as a partisan accusation to volley, but as a sensation that burrows beneath politics and ideology. The current conversation around AI and data centers, for example, feels less like a partisan debate than one about basic human priorities. The discomfort that people feel with a technology that is encroaching into more and more areas of life, and the sense, even if slightly inchoate, that something crucial is being taken away from us—this is the beginning of moral understanding, the basis for moral language. You don’t need theology for it. Neiman wants us to call out evil because she believes that doing so is the only way to call forth its opposite, an awareness and exaltation of the good. For her, this would mean liberals rediscovering principles that felt particularly absent in the age of wokeness, and even long before that: “the commitment to universalism over tribalism, the distinction between justice and power, and the belief in the possibility of progress.” The politicians who start championing these principles—and some are beginning to—might find a receptive audience. They speak to desires and impulses that persist beneath the nihilism that floods our communication channels and weighs down our souls. If you need further convincing, Neiman writes, just think of how strange Trump appears to us. In many ways, it’s his absence of moral impulse, his unabashedness, that makes him such a fascinating and compelling character. We don’t normally come across individuals like this in our lives and in our communities, where people more often than not selflessly help one another—he feels anomalous. “Might this itself be a refutation of the self-interested power paradigm we are told is universally true?” Neiman writes. “A world in which that model was truly universal would be a world in which everyone behaved like Donald Trump.” This is, thankfully, not our world, and we can find solace in being reminded that most people, at bottom, do recognize what morality looks like. They live it every day. If only our politics could be guided by the same instinct.

items.title: A Wolf Dawg’s Tale
items.description: Imagine reaching into a closet for a shirt, or maybe a sheet, and instead making contact with what feels like a dead ferret. It’s furry, but instead of soft and fluffy, it’s hard and grimy, like it hasn’t been cleaned in 18 years. Because it hasn’t. Because it is my husband Ian’s college Halloween costume, the one he has worn nearly every year of his adult life, in four cities and nine different homes. It is Wolf Dawg. And I can’t convince him to get rid of it. Wolf Dawg is not a reference. There is no Wolf Dawg cinematic universe and there is no Wolf Dawg meme, or at least there wasn’t when my husband bought the costume at a thrift shop near Ohio State, in 2008. It is not a wolf, nor is it a dog. It is a silky, polyester, stop-sign-red shirt with WOLF DAWG emblazoned on the chest, in what I can only describe as a Halloween typeface. But its hallmark is its arms: those coarse, furry brown arms. The whole thing is decrepit now—and, my husband assures me, would surely disintegrate in the wash—but it was already falling apart when he got it, with little pills all over and runs at the collar. Still: It was, he told me, “love at first sight.” My first reaction to seeing Wolf Dawg was mild repulsion. My husband was almost 30 when we started dating, which now I see as young, but at the time I saw as old enough to know better. Call me a misandrist, but to my mind, there’s something unbecoming about a grown man wearing a cheap novelty Halloween costume, let alone such a bad one. That the costume didn’t give me enough of the ick to leave is a testament, I think, to how much I’d already fallen in love with him. Sweet, innocent, 27-year-old me: I didn’t consider that I’d be sharing precious closet space with Wolf Dawg for the rest of my life. [ Read: Trick-or-treating isn’t what it used to be ] The weirdest part about this is that my husband is an obsessive culler and refresher. Of the two of us, I am the hoarder. My mother grew up in China, during an economically depressed era, and even after making plenty of money, she was the kind of parent who couldn’t imagine spending $20 on new towels when the crunchy ones worked just fine. My husband has taught me to recognize abundance when I have it, to spend for joy and not only for need. He buys my favorite overpriced pastries just for the sake of it, and he has lightly shamed me into buying new sneakers when the old ones—although technically wearable—have worn-down treads. I also may be the only woman in America whose husband buys more new clothes than she does. Ian Stroud Ian Stroud Wolf Dawg wasn’t intended to be a forever costume. My husband can’t quite recall what drew him to it, but like many 21-year-old men in the early aughts, he was into CollegeHumor and owned a shirt of the company’s that said the right to bear arms and featured an illustration of a man with literal bear arms. Wolf Dawg’s striking resemblance to that man might have been part of the appeal. Yet from the beginning, my husband understood that Wolf Dawg would stand alone. It came with a fuzzy-eared hat, which he tossed immediately. “I didn’t want to wear a dorky hat,” he said. “Wolf Dawg is cool. That hat was lame.” The first year he wore it, his friends were all a little confused. “The initial assumption was Oh, Wolf Dawg is a werewolf ,” his college buddy Brady told me. “But no, Ian would insist it’s just Wolf Dawg.” Nobody understood it, because there was nothing to understand. The second year he wore it, his friends considered it a matter of thrift: Sure, why not get your money’s worth? “But year three rolled around,” Brady said, “and it became clear this would be the only costume he’d ever wear again.” [ Read: The chronically online have stolen Halloween ] My husband had a sincere reason for the annual ritual. Modern adult Halloween, he said, is exhausting: a Sisyphean pursuit of cleverness and terrible pun-based costumes about current events, as if the worst of social-media discourse was forcing itself into regular parties—all faux intellectualism and very little celebration of artistry, craft, or horror. Wolf Dawg was commentary. Wolf Dawg was easy. Wolf Dawg was clean, if not physically then at least socially. “I don’t have to participate, but I can participate,” he said. “I never had to try and win.” When people asked what the costume was, he’d simply respond, “You know: Wolf Dawg,” as if they’d asked him who Spider-Man was. The costume became legend among his friends. At some point, Brady remembers it changing from Wolf Dawg to Guy Who Is Dressed as Wolf Dawg, which only added to the lore: “This guy is so excited about his half-ass costume that is fully labeled—the name right there on the shirt—and he still has to explain it to everyone.” My husband reveled in being a contrarian and would pursue a joke even if it made only him laugh. “I think he knew some people might be confused and annoyed,” Brady said, “and that was funny to him.” The truth is, though, that Wolf Dawg persisted for one important reason: girls. The ladies loved Wolf Dawg. They’d come up and ask to pet the arms. Sometimes they wouldn’t even ask. “It was insane,” Brady confirmed. Any party, every party—in off-campus apartments in Columbus, Ohio; in dingy New York City bars; even at a crowded comedy show in Washington, D.C. Wolf Dawg is likely coated in the pungent remnants of dozens (dozens!) of beer-pong games. The girls apparently touched that grubby fur all the same. Most days, my husband struggled to approach women. But for one night a year, here was Wolf Dawg: the ultimate wingman, inviting women to discover his most charming and silly self. Ian Stroud By the time I met my husband, Wolf Dawg’s peak wingman days were over, or maybe I initiated its demise. But in case it’s not already obvious, my husband loves a gag, and Wolf Dawg is his longest-running one. I also don’t actually need him to get rid of it, as much as I would love to avoid the jump scare during spring cleaning. I didn’t even realize that Wolf Dawg had never been washed until I asked him about it for this article, because my husband does most of the laundry. (And the cleaning. And, while we’re at it, probably more of the child care too.) The man I know wouldn’t typically let something so objectively gross remain in our home. My husband does seem like a different person in the old Wolf Dawg photos. In them, he still has all of his hair, which he’d lost long before we met. He’s drinking, which he stopped doing a few years ago. He’s smirking, a little self-satisfied. That young man felt compelled to make a statement, felt a need to impress in his own way. He believed that traditions were dumb, that the institution of marriage was a farce, that he’d never have kids, that he had nothing to lose and everything to say. [ Read: Adult Halloween is stupid, embarrassing, and very important ] Now he’s never the first person to announce his opinion. He’s thoughtful. He trusts his own point of view, yet has no interest in persuading everybody around him to conform to his beliefs. He has less to prove. (He also, thankfully, has graduated from some of the most cringey aspects of 2010s Millennial humor.) I have trouble envisioning the version of my husband that the pictures reveal. Really, I owe Wolf Dawg. Perhaps my husband wouldn’t have gained the confidence he has today had he not slipped into the costume. Perhaps I wouldn’t be married to him if not for all the young women who caressed those fur arms. Ever since we met, he has been transforming, as I have. Every year that he puts on Wolf Dawg, the distance between who he was and who he is grows. In this way, Halloween is exactly the ritual it should be: a commemoration of time’s passage—an honoring of who we were, and who we have yet to become. Deteriorating polyester and all.

items.title: FC AshantiGold CEO calls for separate Black Stars team for home-based players
items.description: FC AshantiGold CEO, Edward Akuoko, has backed the inclusion of locally-based players in the Black Stars urging Ghana to develop a pool of home-based talents capable of stepping in whenever key players of the national team are unavailable. Mr. Akuoko believes Ghana must establish a deliberate system to identify, develop and integrate players from the domestic league into the senior national team to ensure continuity and consistency. Speaking to Luv FM, he said: “We can have a local Black Stars team, and then we can have the foreign base as well, and then we can always blend them so that whenever the foreign ones are not available, the local ones can step in. “I think that history has it that we’ve done this before and it worked for Ghana. A time came when we had a local Black stars that was playing so well to the point that there were times that even the local black stars were even playing much better than even the foreign ones.” According to him, building a reliable pool of locally based players would provide the Black Stars with quality alternatives whenever first-choice players are unavailable due to injuries, suspension other circumstances. “One thing is that when you use the local black stars, first of all, you are able to build cohesion because they are always available at your best and core. “These foreign players sometimes, through no fault of theirs, are not consistent. And we all know that football, to a large extent, is about consistency. I mean, when players are able to play together, train together. “The the the cohesion comes and they’re able to play well. And so if we’re having challenges, I think that it’s not a bad idea,” he added.

items.title: Lahore ATC denies police further remand of PTI's Hammad Azhar, sends him on judicial remand
items.description: LAHORE: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Tuesday rejected a police request for further physical remand of PTI leader Hammad Azhar in the Jinnah House attack case and sent him to jail on judicial remand. Sarwar Road police had booked several PTI leaders and workers on charges of attacking and vandalising Jinnah House during the May 9, 2023 protests against the arrest of former prime minister Imran Khan. According to his family , Azhar was arrested on Sept 5. However, police said the next day they were unaware of his arrest, and he was produced before an ATC on Sept 7. His initial 21-day physical remand was extended at least twice . Subsequently, upon the completion of the latest 12-day remand, the PTI leader was presented before ATC Judge Sardar Muhammad Akram Khan on Tuesday. The investigating officer sought further physical remand of the former finance minister, stating that the police wanted to conduct a polygraph test , also known as a lie detector test. However, Azhar’s counsel, Barrister Abuzar Salman Niazi, argued that a polygraph test required the suspect’s consent. He argued that according to a Lahore High Court judgment , the procedure was to be conducted during judicial remand. The lawyer said the suspect was also required to make a statement before a magistrate indicating whether he wished to undergo the test. Azhar told the court that he did not want to undergo the test if the law allowed him to refuse it. He said a suspect should not be punished for the prosecution’s alleged lack of knowledge about the legal requirements. After hearing arguments from the prosecution and the defence over the proposed polygraph test, Judge Akram dismissed the police request for further physical remand and sent Azhar to jail under judicial custody. Barrister Niazi hailed the verdict, writing on X that his client’s “50-day physical remand finally ends” and that he was sent to Kot Lakhpat jail. Azhar served as a federal minister for multiple portfolios during the PTI government, including finance, industries and energy . In the aftermath of the May 2023 riots, when the state launched a crackdown against the party leadership, he had gone into hiding and reappeared in public a year later, on May 22, 2024. In 2025, he reiterated his decision to step down as the president of the PTI’s Punjab chapter, citing a lack of access to Imran.

items.title: Deux suspects interpellés pour trafic présumé d’ossements humains
items.description: La gendarmerie nationale du Cameroun a interpellé, les 20 et 21 octobre 2026, deux individus qui sont soupçonnés d’être impliqués dans un présumé trafic d’ossements humains, selon un communiqué de la force sécuritaire, ce mardi 27 octobre. «Les 20 et 21 octobre 2026, les éléments de la Compagnie de Gendarmerie de Yokadouma ont interpellé deux individus soupçonnés d’implication dans un présumé trafic d’ossements humains», lit-on dans le communiqué de l’institution sécuritaire, ce mardi 27 octobre. Selon la gendarmerie, c’est «à la suite d’un renseignement», que «les éléments de l’unité de céans, conduits par le Chef d’Escadron Russel Fonkou MBa, ont interpellé le premier suspect, le 20 octobre 2026». C’est ainsi qu’il a été découvert «un sac contenant des ossements humains, dans un champ situé derrière son domicile au quartier Paradis». La gendarmerie camerounaise déclare que «selon les premiers éléments de l’enquête, les ossements étaient destinés à être écoulés dans les villes de Yokadouma et de Bertoua». Cela a conduit également à une deuxième interpellation, un présumé complice du premier, le 21 octobre 2026. «L’enquête révèle que les deux présumés trafiquants d’ossements humains auraient, avec le concours de membres de la communauté Baka, déterré les ossements d’une vieille dame appartenant à cette communauté, dans la localité de Sengbot PK 72, située dans la circonscription de l’unité», poursuit la gendarmerie. La force sécuritaire affirme que «les ossements saisis ont été placés sous scellés et seront transmis, avec les pièces de procédure, à Monsieur le Procureur de la République près les tribunaux d’instance de Yokadouma». Par Wakat Séra L’article Deux suspects interpellés pour trafic présumé d’ossements humains est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Ghanaian twins plead guilty in US$9m international romance scam
items.description: Two Ghanaian twin brothers have pleaded guilty in the United States to conspiracy to commit wire fraud in an international romance scam that caused victims to lose more than US$9 million. Jamal Abubakari and Kamal Abubakari, both 22, entered their guilty pleas on October 13, 2026. They allegedly operated under the aliases Arrangement and Lancaster, respectively. Their co-conspirator, 53-year-old American woman Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie, also known as Amanda Joy Glum and Amanda Joy Kessei Bierman, pleaded guilty to the same offence on October 20. According to the US Department of Justice, the three were involved in a criminal network that targeted older Americans through dating websites and social media between July 2024 and April 2026. The group allegedly created false identities to build close relationships with victims, presenting some of the interactions as romantic relationships. They then used fabricated stories to persuade the victims to transfer money into accounts controlled by members of the network, with some of the proceeds sent to accomplices in Ghana and elsewhere. The scheme affected victims in 25 US states, as well as Germany and Austria. Some of those affected in northern Ohio were residents of Edgerton in Williams County. The total financial losses exceeded US$9 million. As part of their plea agreements, the three defendants have agreed to forfeit jewellery seized during their arrests, including luxury watches, rings, chains, medallions and earrings. The investigation was led by the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Cleveland Division, with support from the US Department of Justice’s Office of International Affairs and law enforcement agencies in Ghana and the United States. Ghanaian agencies involved included the Attorney-General’s Office, the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO), the Ghana Police Service, the Cyber Security Authority, the Narcotics Control Commission, the Financial Intelligence Centre, the Ghana Immigration Service and the National Intelligence Bureau. Each defendant faces a maximum prison sentence of 20 years. A federal district court judge will determine the final sentences after considering the US Sentencing Guidelines and other relevant legal factors.

items.title: Tribunal de commerce de Conakry : « C’est ensemble que nous ferons de cette juridiction une référence », affirme Kaman Magloire Théophile Kouadio
items.description: Nommé le 21 octobre dernier, le juge Kaman Magloire Théophile Kouadio a officiellement pris fonction en tant que président du Tribunal de commerce de Conakry, ce lundi 26 octobre 2026. Il succède à Sékou Kandé, qui prend désormais la présidence de la chambre civile et économique de la Cour d’appel de Conakry. Dans son discours de prise de fonction, le nouveau président du Tribunal de commerce a exprimé sa volonté de préserver les acquis de son prédécesseur et de poursuivre le travail engagé. « Je mesure l’ampleur de l’héritage et je m’engage à le préserver et à le faire fructifier. Soyez assuré de ma reconnaissance et de mon estime : le Tribunal de commerce gardera toujours une place de choix pour vous », a-t-il déclaré. Le magistrat a également souligné le rôle stratégique de cette juridiction dans le fonctionnement de l’économie nationale. « Il est le juge de la vie économique : celui qui tranche les litiges entre commerçants, accompagne les entreprises en difficulté et garantit la sécurité des transactions », a-t-il expliqué. Évoquant le cadre juridique de l’Organisation pour l’harmonisation en Afrique du droit des affaires (OHADA), dont la Guinée est membre, il a rappelé la contribution de la justice commerciale à la sécurisation des investissements et au développement économique. « Un investisseur ne s’installe durablement que là où il sait que son contrat sera respecté et que son litige sera tranché rapidement, équitablement et en toute indépendance », a-t-il affirmé. Pour réussir sa mission, Kaman Magloire Théophile Kouadio a enfin appelé à la mobilisation et à la collaboration de l’ensemble des acteurs de la juridiction. « C’est ensemble, dans un esprit d’équipe, de respect mutuel et de loyauté, que nous ferons du Tribunal de commerce de Conakry une juridiction de référence », a-t-il conclu. Elisa Camara L’article Tribunal de commerce de Conakry : « C’est ensemble que nous ferons de cette juridiction une référence », affirme Kaman Magloire Théophile Kouadio est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Niger miners’ deaths: Committee recommends N1.4bn compensation, dismissal of personnel
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi & Enitan Abdultawab The independent ministerial committee investigating the recent deaths of 33 persons in the custody of the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps NSCDC in Minna, Niger State, has recommended compensation amounting to N1.4 billion to families of the victims. In the Executive Summary by the chairman of the Committee, Jonathan Kure, on Tuesday in Abuja when he presented the report to the Minister of Interior, Hon. Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, the committee, which said the deaths were “entirely preventable”, also recommended summary dismissal of personnel whose actions directly caused the deaths of the suspects. It partly reads, “The committee recommends a restitution of the NSCDCD in order to carry out their reforms. The NDSCD also recommends a restitutive package, a compensation of 30m for each of the 33 bereaved families and 10m to each of the 41 survivors, representing a total compensation package of 1.4 billion naira.” “Additional measures include educational support for dependents of deceased victims, medical rehabilitation of survivors, psychological support for affected families, and a formal apology by the federal government.” It recommended administrative sanctions for personnel who failed in their duties but whose actions or inactions were not directly responsible for the deaths. It added that “fatalities resulted from environmental asphyxia caused by oroloneged confinement in a severely overcrowded cell aggravated by heat stress and dehydration.” According to the committee, the operation which led to the arrest of the suspects was without an “operational order” or approval from the national headquarters of the NSCDC. items.title: Court ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍‌‌‍​⁠​​‌‌​adjourns El-Rufai’s N1bn rights suit against ICPC, AGF, IGP for judgment
items.description: The Federal High Court in Abuja on Tuesday fixed Dec. 2 for judgment in an N1 billion fundamental rights suit filed by former Gov. Nasir El-Rufai of Kaduna State against the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC). Justice Joyce Abdulmalik fixed the date after lawyers and the parties adopted their processes in the case. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that other respondents in the suit are the Inspector-General (I-G) of Police and the Attorney-General of the Federation (AGF) as the 2nd and 3rd respondents, respectively. When the case was called on Tuesday, El-Rufai’s lawyer was not in court. Justice Abdulmalik then made an order deeming all the processes filed by the former governor adopted. Abdul Mohammed, SAN, who appeared for the ICPC, identified and adopted all their processes, urging the court to dismiss the suit in its entirety. The I-G’s lawyer, ACP Ezekiel Rimamsomte, and Mrs Maimuna Lami-Shiru, Director of Civil Litigation and Public Law, who represented the AGF, equally adopted their separate processes and prayed the court to dismiss the suit. While the proceeding was ongoing, Mr Ubong Akpan, the ex-governor’s counsel, entered the courtroom and apologised for his lateness. When the lawyer sought the permission of the court to allow him to adopt his court’s documents, he was informed by the judge that his processes had already been deemed adopted. Justice Abdulmalik consequently adjourned the matter until Dec. 2 for judgment. NAN reports that the ex-governor had, earlier in the suit, sued the ICPC, the Chief Magistrate at the Magistrate’s Court of the FCT, Abuja; I-G and the AGF as 1st to 4th respondents, respectively. He, however, dropped the name of the magistrate from the case following his inability to specify the name of the magistrate who was sued as the 2nd respondent after the judge made the observation. El-Rufai is, therefore, demanding a N1 billion in damages against ICPC, the I-G and the AGF. The former governor, in the originating motion on notice marked FHC/ABJ/CS/345/2026, dated and filed Feb. 20 by Oluwole Iyamu, SAN, sought seven reliefs. He prayed the court to declare that the invasion and search of his residence at House 12, Mambilla Street, Aso Drive, Abuja, on Feb. 19 at about 2pm by the ICPC and I-G amounts to a gross violation of the applicant’s fundamental rights. He said that it was a violation of the dignity of the human person, personal liberty, fair hearing, and privacy under Sections 34, 35, 36, and 37 of the Constitution.” He urged the court to declare that “any evidence obtained pursuant to the aforesaid invalid warrant and unlawful search is inadmissible in any proceedings against the applicant, as it was procured in breach of constitutional safeguards.” El-Rufai, therefore, sought an order of injunction restraining the respondents and their agents from further relying on, using, or tendering any evidence or items seized during the unlawful search in any investigation, prosecution, or proceedings involving him. He sought an order directing the 1st and 3rd respondents (ICPC and I-G) to forthwith return all items seized from the applicant’s premises during the unlawful search, together with a detailed inventory thereof. He also sought an order awarding the sum of N1,000,000,000.00 (one billion naira) as general, exemplary, and aggravated damages, among others. Responding, in its counter-affidavit, the ICPC said it received a petition against El-Rufai, and acting on the petition, it commenced an investigation, leading to the search at his residence. It argued that its operatives acted under a valid search warrant issued on Feb. 18 and executed on Feb. 19 between 1:37pm and 3:56pm at 12 Mambilla Street, Asokoro, Abuja. The commission said its officials were accompanied by personnel of the Nigeria Police Force and that the exercise was witnessed by El-Rufai’s wife, Hadiza El-Rufai, and his son, Mohammed El-Rufai. The ICPC, which urged the court to dismiss the suit, listed the items allegedly recovered from the residence. The I-G, also in his counter affidavit deposed to by Insp Ewa Anthony, argued that he had the statutory power to detect, arrest, investigate and prosecute offenders. He argued that the search carried out at El-Rufai’s residence was executed pursuant to a search warrant issued by a competent court of law. He disagreed with the ex-governor that the search warrant was invalid, insisting that it was a genuine court order. The police boss said that his officers who carried out the operation complied with all applicable legal procedures in the execution of the search warrant. According to him, the applicant is trying to use the honourable court to shield him away from the security investigation and prosecution in the court of law. He, therefore, prayed the court to dismiss the suit in its entirety. The AGF, in his counter affidavit filed by Lami-Shiru, denied being privy to the facts of the alleged matter. He argued that the ICPC and I-G acted within their statutory functions. According to him, the items seized from the applicant (El-Rufai) by the 1st and 2nd respondents were seized to enable them to conclude an investigation on the applicant. He submitted that the suit was an abuse of court processes because the former governor had two pending suits on the same subject matter before the FCT High Court. The AGF, who argued that El-Rufai’s suit lacked merit, as there is no legal and evidential justification to support all the claims and reliefs sought by him, prayed the court to dismiss it in its entirety. items.title: Adu-Boahene case: Court adjourns motion challenging prosecution’s account of evidence to Thursday
items.description: The High Court in Accra has adjourned to Thursday, October 29, a motion alleging that the prosecution in the Kwabena Adu-Boahene trial misrepresented witness testimony and documentary evidence in its written submissions. The application, filed on October 19, asks the court to strike out passages in the prosecution’s response to the accused persons’ submission of no case to answer, which they contend are unsupported by the trial record. At Monday’s hearing, October 26, the judge said the case docket was at his home and that he had only become aware of the motion that morning. The Attorney-General’s Office, which was reportedly served with the application on October 19, had not filed a formal response as of Monday’s hearing. Thursday’s proceedings will take place ahead of the court’s scheduled November 5 ruling on the substantive submission of no case to answer. Kwabena Adu-Boahene, Angela Adjei Boateng and Advantage Solutions Limited filed the motion through their lawyer, Samuel Atta Akyea. They also filed a separate reply to the prosecution’s opposition to their submission of no case to answer. The two filings serve different purposes. The reply challenges the prosecution’s legal arguments for requiring the accused persons to open their defence, while the motion seeks to have specific passages removed on the grounds that they allegedly misstate the evidence presented at trial. Six areas of disputed evidence In his supporting affidavit, Adu-Boahene identifies six categories of statements in the prosecution’s submissions that the applicants say contradict or are not supported by witness testimony and documentary evidence. One concerns the prosecution’s assertion that two witnesses testified that a purchase agreement and an invoice relating to a cyber-defence system were not genuine. The applicants argue that neither witness gave the testimony attributed to them concerning the purchase agreement, admitted as Exhibit X. They note that the second prosecution witness was discharged on April 27, 2026, while the agreement was admitted through the fourth witness on June 22. On the disputed invoices, the affidavit quotes the second witness as saying: “My Lord, it is likely one will be an error.” It also cites her subsequent explanation that she could not determine which invoice contained the error. The applicants contend that these answers do not support the prosecution’s characterisation of the documents as forged or fabricated. A second complaint concerns the prosecution’s assertion that the second witness testified that the National Signals Bureau had no contract with ISC Holdings Limited for a cyber-defence system. According to the affidavit, the witness gave no such evidence and instead acknowledged processing and paying an invoice covering delivery and acceptance milestones for the system. The motion also challenges the prosecution’s interpretation of the witness’s knowledge of an operations account. The applicants say she repeatedly explained that her security clearance did not permit her to know about certain national security accounts and activities. They argue that her testimony cannot support the broader assertion that the institution itself was unaware of the company or its account. Another disputed passage describes a March 2020 invoice as covering a one-time purchase. The affidavit cites testimony in which the witness acknowledged that the amount under discussion was not the full payment and that another invoice relating to the same acquisition had been processed. The application further challenges the prosecution’s assertion that the entire GH¢49.1 million was spent on the accused persons, their friends, associates and families, with none used for an official or approved purpose. The applicants say the third prosecution witness gave no such evidence. They point instead to testimony identifying ISC International Security Consultants Holdings Limited as the beneficiary of two exhibits, with remittance information referring to the procurement of a cyber-defence system. The sixth complaint concerns the prosecution’s reliance on Exhibit H to support an assertion that payments were made from Advantage Solutions Limited’s bank account to Adu-Boahene’s mother for a building project in Kumasi. Exhibit H, a copy of which is attached to the motion, is a photograph of a building. The applicants argue that it contains no banking or accounting information establishing the alleged payments. Their affidavit also cites the fourth prosecution witness as acknowledging that there were “no direct payments from accounts analysed towards Dorchester Heights”, the building identified as the Kumasi project. Applicants allege prosecution presented unsupported claims The applicants argue that introducing facts unsupported by evidence through written submissions amounts to giving evidence from the bar. They contend that the court should remove the disputed passages because they allegedly misrepresent the evidence on record. The prosecution’s October 9 submissions, signed by Deputy Attorney-General Dr Justice Srem-Sai, maintain that sufficient evidence has been presented to establish the essential elements of the offences. The prosecution argues that its case rests substantially on documentary evidence that was not undermined by the defence’s cross-examination and has asked the court to dismiss the submission of no case to answer. Those submissions predate the motion and do not directly address its specific allegations. The prosecution’s failure to file a formal response by Monday does not, in itself, establish the applicants’ claims. The court is expected to hear the application on Thursday, ahead of its November 5 ruling on whether the accused persons have a case to answer.

items.title: Burkina | Santé : Novembre, mois de la sensibilisation sanitaire dans les langues nationales
items.description: Le ministre de la Santé, le Dr Lucien Jean Claude Kargougou, a animé une conférence de presse ce mardi 27 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou. L'objectif était d'annoncer le lancement officiel du Mois de la communication sanitaire en langues nationales, prévu pour le mois de novembre. Cette rencontre avec les hommes et les femmes des médias, dont le décor a été planté en langues nationales (mooré et dioula), vise à rapprocher l'information sanitaire des populations grâce aux langues locales et aux radios de proximité, afin de susciter un changement de comportement. Placée sous le slogan « La santé vient à vous dans votre langue, sur votre radio ! », cette campagne entend renforcer la sensibilisation à travers des émissions interactives. À cet effet, 95 radios de proximité sont mobilisées pour relayer les sensibilisations et les informations sur la santé. Le ministre Kargougou expliquant le choix des langues nationales Selon le ministre de la Santé, Lucien Jean Claude Kargougou, le ministère organisera, durant la première semaine de novembre, une semaine de redévabilité de son institution. Les trois semaines restantes seront consacrées à des émissions interactives dans les régions, avec les personnels de santé, dans les langues nationales locales. Ces émissions permettront aux citoyens de s'informer, d'exprimer leurs préoccupations et d'échanger avec des spécialistes sur les problématiques de santé qui touchent leurs communautés, dans leur langue. items.title: Elevate Africa calls for stronger partnerships to unlock Africa’s development potential
items.description: Elevate Africa has called for stronger connections between the continent’s resources, capital, leadership and opportunities to accelerate development and translate Africa’s potential into tangible results. The call was made at a press conference in Accra ahead of the Elevate Africa Annual Convening 2026, which will be held under the theme “Africa: Defining Her Future.” Co-founder of Elevate Africa, Her Majesty Olori Atuwatsé III, said the continent already had solutions to many of its challenges but needed greater confidence in its ability to implement them. “Africa doesn’t lack solutions. What we lack is the conviction and the confidence in the solutions that we already have,” she said. She said the organisation was working to promote African-led solutions, bring leaders and creators together, and develop talent through its fellowship programme. Elevate Africa Chief Partnership Officer, Dr Rex Idaminabo, said the continent needed to strengthen the links between its existing resources and the capital, leadership and opportunities required to turn its potential into practical outcomes. “Africa does not lack potential. What Africa needs are stronger connections between its resources, capital, leadership, and opportunities,” he said. The organisation is positioning its annual convening as a platform for bringing together people and institutions to discuss how African resources, ideas and talent can be mobilised to shape the continent’s future. The 2026 edition will be held under the theme “Africa: Defining Her Future.”

Adarkwa’s side are in the last 16 of the tournament following their return after failing to appear in the last three editions prior to this year’s competition. Now that we’ve done that, we want to push Argentina to one side and keep going. items.title: Probe panel blames miners’ deaths on overcrowding, extreme heat, dehydration
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi The independent ministerial committee investigating the recent deaths of 33 persons in the custody of the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Minna, Niger State, has unravelled the cause of death of the suspects. In the Executive Summary by the chairman of the Committee, Jonathan Kure, on Tuesday in Abuja, when he presented the report to the Minister of Interior, Hon. Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, the committee cited the causes of death to include “overcrowding, unsuitable detention condition, failure of duty of care, inadequate supervision”. It reads, “The committee concluded that the incident was a preventable custodial tragedy caused by severe overcrowding, unlawful and unsuitable detention conditions, failure of duty of care, disregard of repeated distress warnings, inadequate supervision, and wider systemic deficiencies. “The evidence did not support claims that the death resulted from a disease outbreak. Available medical and forensic evidence instead indicated that the fatalities resulted from an environmental aphasia, an acute respiratory failure caused by prolonged confinement in a severely overcrowded and poorly ventilated detention cell, aggravated by heat stress and dehydration. “The investigation included interviews with NACDC leadership, operational personnel, cell guards, medical staff, survivors, bereaved families, community representatives, and graveside managers. It also involved examination of arrest and detention registers, communication records, duty rosters, AZB registers, hospital and mortuary records, autopsy findings, and burial records. 29 of the 41 survivors were interviewed, including nine minors. “Evidence from multiple independent sources was analysed and cross-checked to reconstruct events and determine responsibility. The committee established that the tragedy stemmed from enforcement operations against suspected illegal mining activities in and around Minna” According to the committee, the operation which led to the arrest of the suspects was without an “operational order” or approval from the national headquarters of the NSCDC. The post Probe panel blames miners’ deaths on overcrowding, extreme heat, dehydration appeared first on Vanguard News .
